An Administrator who wants other wording edits the page in the editor: the site never rewrites a page it has made. Both pages stay on the site when the plugin is deleted, as every page the plugin makes does.

Putting the copy in first. The pages are made published, so the moment the box is turned on, or the command runs, the welcome email, the Student Report Card and the registration form's confirmation link them. To have the program lead's copy in place before that, run wp wpcredits start_pages while the box is still off, set both pages to Draft in the editor straight away, put the copy in, publish them, and only then turn the box on. A Draft page at the address is used as it is, and a page is linked only while it is published, so nothing points at a Draft page: the Student Report Card leaves its link out, the welcome email leaves its line out, and the confirmation leaves out the Team Matcher mention.

Where the pages are linked. The Student Report Card shows New here? Start here for your first week. under its resources while the Start here page is published. The student welcome email carries a line with the page's address, Your first week, step by step:, through the optional placeholder {start_here_link} (see Tools > Emails); the line is left out while the page is not published. The registration form's confirmation mentions the Team Matcher page while it is published. An email an Administrator had edited before keeps its text, and the shipped text shows as changed in Tools > Emails.

Cohort planning

How many students one mentor takes (since 1.123.68), on the Students and mentors tab, in the section Cohort planning.

  • Students per mentor - a number from 1 to 20, 3 unless changed. The cohort timeline on the Administrator Dashboard counts this many places for each active mentor, and says a month is short when its students are more than the places.

Mentor applications

The form people apply to mentor through, at /become-a-mentor/, since 1.122.31.

  • Applications from mentors - Take mentor applications through the form on this site. Off by default, since it is a public page anybody can post to; its address is under the switch. Every application is stored for an Administrator to decide on the Mentors screen's Waiting for review tab, and the form writes nothing to Airtable; while this is off, the page shows one sentence saying applications are closed, and an Administrator who opens it a second saying why (until 1.123.26 the public were shown nothing here, and on the institution and sponsor forms too, whatever their rows said). As with the other forms, its consent box links to the WordPress.org privacy policy, not to this site's own privacy page (since 1.123.24), and the row's fold says so.
  • Make mentors from applications (since 1.122.33) - Make a mentor of each selected applicant whose course shows, or for whom The course is completed is pressed. Off until the launch, since on means accounts made, invitations sent and rows written in the shared Airtable base, which somebody decides on the day rather than an update deciding it. Its fold: while it is off, an applicant whose course shows waits under Selected (course pending). What it does, and what the launch asks of a person beforehand, is under Applications to mentor in the part on the plugin in wp-admin.
  • Who is mailed - the addresses told of each new mentor application, chosen as the Institutions tab's reviewers are; with none here, every Administrator is written to. The email names the applicant and their WordPress.org profile and links the Waiting for review tab; it carries none of their other answers. Point it at your own address before you try the form, or every Administrator hears of the test.
  • Mentors' course invitation link - the link the selection email gives a selected applicant to join the mentors' course. Its fold: Select is refused while it is empty, since the selection email would have no link to give, and only an https link is kept.
  • Selected applications lapse after (days) - from 14 to 365, 90 by default: a selected applicant whose course has not shown after this many days is moved to Lapsed with a dated note, and Select is offered on the row again.

The Institutions tab

Six sections, headed on the screen Applications and enrollment, Areas of responsibility, Landing page, When an institution leaves the pipeline, Collaboration Agreements and Semester reports.

Institution applications and enrollment

  • Applications from institutions - Take applications through the form on this site. Off by default, since the form is a public page anybody can post to; its address is under the switch. Since 1.123.27 the form is at /institution-application/, titled "Bring WordPress Credits to your institution", and /apply/, its address before, takes a visitor there. Every submission is stored for an Administrator to read on the Institutions screen's Waiting for review tab and to decide on the Administrator Dashboard, and nothing is created until somebody approves it; while this is off, the page shows one sentence saying applications are closed. Since 1.123.24 the form's consent box links to the WordPress.org privacy policy, not to the page chosen under Settings > Privacy, so the form no longer waits on this site having a privacy page, and the row's fold says which policy it links. Since 1.123.29 the form also asks the contact's role at the institution and, from the mentor form's list, the languages the students study in, both required, and under The agreement, who will sign it for the institution, their title and the institution's page about WordPress Credits, none of them required, though a title is asked for when somebody is named to sign and a name when a title is given. These five answers are kept on this site and never sent to Airtable. On approval they are copied to a record of the institution on this site, kept under its Airtable record ID, so they are still there once the application has been deleted. When the approval joins a record the program already had, they fill only what that record does not hold yet, and a second press of Approve changes nothing. If the site cannot keep them, the approval stops before the application is called approved, the Airtable record and the account already made stay, and pressing Approve again finishes it. An institution approved before 1.123.29 has no such record.
  • Enrollment lists from institutions - Let an institution send a list of students to enroll. Adds an "Enroll students" section to the Institution Dashboard, where a school chooses the program and the term and then adds one student or sends a CSV. Off by default. Beside the file box, a link Download a sample list sends a file, students-sample.csv, with four of the headers the import reads (name, email, field_of_study, tutor) and one example student, so a school that has never seen the format is shown one; the import also reads an optional profile column. Since 1.123.41 the import refuses an address at example.test, the example's domain, as the sample list's own row ("This is the sample list's example student. Replace it with one of your students, or delete the row."), so a sample sent back unchanged creates nobody; the other rows of a file are checked as usual. The site makes the file when the link is followed, to an account that may enroll students, and holds no copy of it. Its fold: the list is read and checked against the program records, and the school sees what was understood before anything is created; while this is off, the section does not appear at all. Each institution is held to five checks an hour and 600 students a day, and the files are read and never stored.
  • Create accounts automatically - Let the sync create the first account for a Confirmed institution, from the Contact Email Airtable holds, and only for a Confirmed institution whose agreement is recorded and that has never had a member. Off by default. Its fold: an address that already belongs to an account is left alone, and on the Institutions screen's Accounts tab, under No account, the institution is listed with the reason, never the address or the account; with this off, accounts are created only when somebody presses Create account there.

Institution areas of responsibility

Which Administrator a new institution is assigned to: the country's own Administrator first, then the region's. An Administrator here is an account with the plugin's manage capability, never every WordPress administrator account.

  • Regions - one choice per region (Africa, Asia, Europe, Latin America and the Caribbean, Middle East, North America, Oceania): the Administrator who has the whole region, or Nobody.
  • Countries - the countries that have their own Administrator, one row each. A country with a row goes to that Administrator whatever its region says; choose Nobody in its row to take it away.
  • Add a country - type a country, choose its Administrator and save. A country that already has its row is refused, naming it and its Administrator, so a country has one Administrator.
  • Who has what - one line per Administrator with an area, such as "Ana: Europe; Poland".
  • Countries by region - closed until opened: each region's countries, and No region for a country the plugin's map does not hold. Move a country puts one in another region; choosing the plugin's own region takes the move away.

A save is refused, and nothing of the areas is saved, when it gives a country to a second Administrator (the sentence names the country and who has it already) or names an account that is not an Administrator. A country or a region with nobody leaves its institutions unassigned. A new application is emailed to its assigned Administrator, and one no area covers to the addresses in Who is emailed about institutions under Collaboration Agreements, or to every Administrator when nobody is named there.

Gaps. The Institutions screen's Pipeline tab lists the countries that institutions name and no area gives an Administrator ("Countries named by institutions with no Administrator in the areas of responsibility"), each with how many institutions, and an institution in one is marked "no area". Give the country, or its region, an Administrator here to close the gap. A change here assigns nobody already on the program: an institution keeps the Administrator it has until somebody reassigns it on its details card. The guide to running the program has the rest, and the command that fills the areas in the first time.

Institution landing page

  • Institution landing page - Use the Institution Dashboard page as the institution dashboard, on by default: institution accounts go to their Institution Dashboard when they log in and in place of the wp-admin Dashboard, with the same exceptions as for mentors and students. Their toolbar link to it is there whether this is on or off. The page's address is under the switch.

Since 1.123.59 the same holds here: an institution account that can write posts still goes to the Institution Dashboard, and only an editor or an administrator stays in wp-admin.

When an institution leaves the pipeline

  • Its people - Remove its people, so they lose access to its students, the default, or Leave their access in place. The accounts themselves are never deleted either way, and the agreement and the roster are kept. Its fold: an institution leaves the pipeline when Airtable moves it out of the stages the program treats as active, which the Advanced tab lists under Pipeline stages.

Collaboration Agreements

  • Agreement review - how many days, from 1 to 60 and 3 by default, a signed agreement or an institution's application may wait before the queue marks it overdue, and an agreement before the nightly reminder names it.
  • Who is emailed about institutions (called Who reviews agreements until 1.123.26, the same setting) - who gets every email about institutions an Administrator is sent: a new application from an institution that no area gives an Administrator, a signed agreement uploaded for review, the nightly reminder of agreements waiting past the review days, the notice that the agreement template cannot be used, an institution's last member leaving, and the three emails about a school's details: a school saving a correction of its contact or agreement details (what changed, from what to what), a school asking to correct its name, website, city, country or contact's email (what it asks for, with a link to the request on the Administrator Dashboard), and a school withdrawing that request. A box for each Administrator, under Administrators, and an Other addresses line for anybody else, separated by commas. To have every Administrator account emailed, tick Mail every Administrator account instead of the people below, above the list; a list with no address in it is refused. While nobody is named, a notice under the field says so: "Nobody is named, so every Administrator account gets these emails." That means every account with the WordPress Administrator role, technical ones too, so name somebody. Where no Administrator account with an email address can be listed, the addresses are typed, separated by commas.
  • The agreement wording - the Google Doc the plugin's copy of the Collaboration Agreement was taken from, linked from the Agreement template card on the Institutions screen's Agreements tab; Google addresses only. Its fold: it is kept on this site rather than in the code, because the document is editable by anyone holding its link and the plugin's source is public.

Semester report drafting

  • Drafting - Draft each institution's semester report when the semester ends, on by default: a daily job drafts a report for every finished semester and tells the Administrators. Off, drafts are written only when an Administrator presses Draft now.
  • Drafting grace - how many days after a semester ends, from 7 to 365 and 45 by default, the job waits for students still in progress before drafting anyway. The draft says how many were still in progress.
  • Who reviews reports - who is told when the job drafts a report, chosen as the agreements' reviewers are. With none, every Administrator is written to.

The Sponsors tab

Six sections, headed on the screen Applications, Landing page, When a sponsor is no longer Approved, Interest mail, Offers and Tiers.

Sponsor applications

  • Applications from sponsors - Take sponsor applications through the form on this site, at /sponsor-application/. Off by default, since it is a public page anybody can post to; its address is under the switch. Every submission is stored for an Administrator to read on the Sponsors screen's Waiting for review tab and to decide on the Administrator Dashboard, and nothing becomes a sponsor until somebody approves it; while this is off, the page shows one sentence saying applications are closed. As with institutions, its consent box links to the WordPress.org privacy policy, and the row's fold says so.

Sponsor landing page

  • Sponsor landing page - Send sponsor accounts to the Sponsor Dashboard when they log in, instead of the wp-admin Dashboard, on by default. Accounts that manage the program, or that can edit other people's posts, editors and administrators, are left where WordPress sends them, and so are mentors. The page's address is under the switch.

When a sponsor is no longer Approved

  • Its accounts - Remove its accounts from the sponsor, so they lose access to its Sponsor Dashboard, or Leave their access in place, the default. Nothing is ever deleted, and Paused and Not Moving Forward sponsors keep their accounts by default, because a pause is often short. Its fold: the status is the record, and the first answer has a status change on the Sponsors screen remove the accounts of a sponsor that is no longer Approved.

Interest mail

  • Who is mailed - the addresses mailed in place of a sponsor's Administrator when it has none, chosen as the Institutions tab's reviewers are; with none here, every Administrator is written to. Every mail meant for a sponsor's Administrator goes to its assigned Administrator: its interests, a mentor it would like to sponsor, its signed agreement, a problem reported with one of its codes, a warning that its codes are running low, the mail thirty days before its term ends and the mails about the events it plans, changes or cancels. A sponsor with none is mailed here, and every new sponsor application comes here too, since a new application has no Administrator yet.

Offers

  • Largest logo - the largest logo file, in KB, from 100 to 8192 and 1024 by default, for the logos sponsors upload and the ones sent with an application. PNG, JPEG and WebP only; never SVG.
  • Tools from our sponsors - two boxes: Show the section on the Student Report Card, on by default, and Show the section on the Mentor Report Card, off by default. The section lists the live offers, each with its claim button. Its fold: a student always sees offers open to students, a mentor sees the offers whose sponsor opened them to mentors, and the Administrator Dashboard shows every live offer whatever these say.
  • Low-stock warning - when a pool of one-time codes falls below this many codes, from 1 to 1000 and 10 by default, the sponsor and its Administrator are mailed, once per crossing. Its fold: this is the default for new offers, and each offer can set its own.

Sponsor tiers

  • Sponsor tiers - Launch the sponsor tiers, the launch switch for the tiers, off by default: ticking it is the launch. Turning it on publishes the Partners page; turning it off returns the page to draft. Its fold lists everything else it turns on. While it is off, the switch gates the Partners page and the Sponsors block (the full list and the strip on the landing page alike), the badge a sponsor puts on its own site, the Handbook listing tab on the Sponsors screen, the application form's Which level are you considering? question, the partnership tiles a track's students see on their Student Report Card and the offers its partners keep for them, the Sponsor Dashboard's Your sponsorship view and its rows under Waiting for you for the term and for a returned event, the Sponsorship, Badge, Reports and Events cards, the reports a sponsor's members open on the Reports card and the event planner on the Events card, the Administrator Dashboard's Events card and its tile, which the Overview lists too, the Events card on the Sponsors screen's Waiting for review tab and the events in its menu bubble, and the Events from our sponsors lists, the reminders the day before each approved event, the description for the partner page, the caps a tier puts on posts, and the dormant state; the daily run puts nothing to dormant and wakes nothing. A signed-in Administrator sees the Partners page and the Sponsors block while the switch is off, under a note that visitors do not see them yet; the badge and the application's tier question stay refused to everyone, Administrators included, and the Handbook listing tab stays out of the Sponsors screen's tab bar, its address opening the first tab, until the switch is on. Administrators can set tiers, terms and funded lines on the Sponsors screen whether it is on or off, the Sponsors screen and the Administrator Dashboard show them either way, and the mail that warns of a term's end thirty days ahead goes out either way. Switched off again after being on, it leaves whatever is dormant where it is until it is back on, and the sponsor reads only that the program is holding it back.
  • Tier grace date - 31 December 2026 by default. On or before this day nothing a sponsor's tier does not cover goes dormant, even with the switch on. Its fold: from the day after, the daily run applies the tiers as set. Until the day has passed, the Sponsors screen says what the run would put to dormant on the day after it. A value that is not a real date leaves the stored day in place.

The Security tab

Two sections, Two-factor authentication and Claude access (MCP).

Two-factor authentication

  • Roles that must use it - a box for each role: Administrators, then Student, Mentor, Institution and Sponsor. An account in a ticked role is asked for a code as well as its password from its next sign-in, with nothing to set up first: the code is emailed. Administrators and institutions by default. Its fold: each person can set up an authenticator app on their own profile screen, which is quicker and does not depend on their email, and unticking everything asks nobody. Students are left off by default: a student account holds that student's own work, there are hundreds of them, and there is nobody to unlock the ones who change phone. They can still turn it on for themselves. Without the Two Factor plugin active nobody is asked, and the row says so above its boxes.
  • Where it stands - while the Two Factor plugin is active, for each ticked role, how many accounts are covered and how many use an authenticator app, counted when the tab is opened. An account that is covered but has no app is using emailed codes.

Claude access (MCP)

Lets the Administrators ticked here ask Claude questions that the site answers from its own records, read-only, through the MCP Adapter plugin. The section is saved with the tab's one Save settings, along with the roles above it.

  • Turn it on - Let Claude read the program's figures. Off by default. Under the box, one sentence says whether the MCP Adapter plugin is active: when it is not, nothing can connect whatever the box says; when it is active but older than 0.7.1, the version Claude access was written against, the sentence names the adapter's version and says Claude access needs 0.7.1 or later, so nothing can connect; when it is active at 0.7.1 or later, the sentence names the adapter's version and the address Claude connects at, the site's /wp-json/mcp/wpcredits. Every field of the section is written on every Save, so change this switch one way at a time: a tab opened before a change made from the command line, and saved afterward, writes the old value back.
  • Who may connect - a box for each account that holds the program's management capability, named "display name (login)", or by the login alone when the account has no display name or its display name is its login, ticked for the accounts that may connect. Nobody by default. An account that is no longer drawn, because it was deleted or is no longer an Administrator, is taken off the list at the next Save; unticking every box empties the list. Under the boxes: each person creates their own application password on their profile, with a name that begins with Claude, for example "Claude - laptop". Its fold: a password with any other name does not open this address, and a password named this way opens nothing else.
  • What the address checks - every request to the address is checked before anything answers, in this order, and the first thing that fails is the answer. No account: refused with 401, and nothing is logged, so a stranger cannot fill the log. The switch off: the address answers 404 and the check asks again all the same. A sign-in that is not an application password named Claude, such as a browser session or a password with any other name: refused with 403. An account that does not hold the program's management capability, or is not ticked under Who may connect: refused with 403. Each refusal of a signed-in account is a row in the log, one for each request however many times WordPress asks about it, and 60 an hour at most for each account; a question refused for being over the hour's, the day's or the lookups' limit counts in the same 60. The other half is the fence: a password named Claude opens this address and nothing else. Used on any other REST route or on the batch route it is refused with 403. On XML-RPC it fails to sign in, and on any other request that is not REST, such as the VideoPress requests Jetpack opens in wp-admin, it counts as nobody being signed in. That holds whether the switch is on or off, and on a REST route the refusal shows in the log as "Refused: another address". A password counts as named Claude when its name begins with Claude, in any case and with spaces before it: "Claude - laptop" does and "Claudette" does not. Before deactivating this plugin or installing a version below 1.123.30, revoke every application password whose name begins with Claude, or check that there is none: without the plugin, such a password opens every address its account can use.
  • Limits - three numbers, each counted per person. Answers an hour, per person is 120 by default and from 1 to 1,000, and Answers a day, per person is 600 by default and from 1 to 10,000; both count across every answer. Lookups of people an hour, per person is 40 by default and from 1 to 200, with a line under its field saying so, and counts only the questions that look people up (A student's tracks, A mentor's students and Mentor applications), on top of the other two: a lookup of people also takes a place of the hour's answers and of the day's. When it is the lookups' limit that is reached, the question is refused with a message that names the limit, for example "The limit of 40 lookups of people an hour is reached.", and the time the hour starts again, and the refusal is logged as "refused: people_limit". That question takes no place of any of the three, and every other question goes on answering. A number outside its range is saved as the nearest end of it.
  • Keep the log for - a number of days, 90 by default and from 7 to 365, outside which it is saved as the nearest end. Every answer and every refusal of a signed-in account is logged and kept for this many days.
  • Latest calls - under the rows, a heading and a table of the newest 100 calls in the log, which the tab only reads and the Save does not touch. A row has When (in the site's date and time formats), Who (the account's display name, or "A removed account" when it has been deleted), Password (the name of the application password the call was signed with, never the password), Asked, Outcome, Rows (how many of the program's records the answer named) and Time taken in milliseconds. Asked is the question's name, for example "Program counts"; "Refused at the door" for a call that was turned away before any question was named, such as a browser session or a password not named Claude; and "Refused: another address" for a Claude password used anywhere but the MCP address. Outcome is answered, failed, or refused with its ground, for example "refused: hour_limit". Nothing asked yet shows "Nothing has been asked yet." instead of the table. A failed answer, and a server the MCP Adapter could not create, also leave one line in PHP's error log, at most one an hour of each, and nothing else: for an answer, the question's name and the exception's class, not_an_answer or invalid_output; for the server, the error's code or the exception's class. The table scrolls inside its own box, which a keyboard reaches. Under it: "See more with wp wpcredits mcp_log." That command lists up to 1,000 calls, newest first, as a table, JSON or CSV (--limit from 1 to 1,000, 100 by default; --format), with the columns when, account (the login), password, ability, outcome, reason, rows and ms; JSON and CSV also give input (what was asked, as JSON) and records (the IDs of the records that went out) after reason. A daily job deletes the calls older than Keep the log for, in batches of 500, the oldest first, up to 10,000 rows a run and the rest the next day, never fewer than 7 days whatever the setting holds, and no other row of the audit trail; it runs whether the switch is on or off.
  • What Claude can ask - seven questions, answered from the records the site already keeps and never from Airtable or WordPress.org. Four give figures and name no person, and each says when its sources were last read (for What waits for an Administrator, when each sync last ran; for Mentor engagement, the moment it counts as of). Program counts gives the figures the Administrator Dashboard counts for the current semester: students per track, mentors, institutions per stage, sponsors per tier, mentor applications and the outcome figures. What waits for an Administrator lists what waits, the counts the Administrator Dashboard reads, with how many wait and where to open each, and when each sync last ran and runs next and whether the Syncs and health card counts it among those that need a look. Mentor engagement says how many active mentors signed in, were seen, acted or stayed idle, as the Engagement tab counts them, as of a day. One institution is found by its record ID or by part of its name, five at most at a time, and gives its pipeline stage, country and city, its Collaboration Agreement's status and dates, how many accounts act for it and its students per group, for one semester or for all, and when the institutions and, separately, the roster behind the students were last read. An institution's contact, the person who accepted its agreement and its members are never named, and every name and label in an answer is cut to one line of at most 120 characters. The other three look people up, in the next point.
  • The three that look people up - A student's tracks, A mentor's students and Mentor applications are the lookups of people that the third limit above counts, and the only questions that do. A student's tracks finds a student by an email address, a WordPress.org username or profile address, a Students record ID or three characters or more of a name, for one institution or for all, and lists ten people at most; for each person, whether they have an account on this site and every track they hold, one for each Students row (a row marked Duplicated or SPAM is never one), with the track's Students record ID, its status, institution, cohort, start and end days, contribution team, hours, how many reports it has, whether a mentor is assigned and that mentor's Mentors record ID, and the course the student took while they wait to graduate. A student with no account on this site has no row on the Student accounts list, and an Administrator puts the name to the ID on an institution's roster instead (see Looking a person up). A mentor's students finds a mentor by a Mentors record ID, a WordPress username, an email address or a WordPress.org profile address, and only a mentor: an account that is not on the Engagement tab is nobody. In both questions, a username is read as one only when it is typed whole, so a name with a letter a username cannot hold finds nobody by username; here a Mentors record ID is also matched letter for letter in its case. It gives the mentor's Mentors record ID, whether the mentor is active, the days of their last sign-in and last visit and the Engagement view they are filed under, and their students as the Mentor Report Card lists them, the current ones before the past ones and 25 at most, each by the Students record ID of the track and with the status, the hours the card prints and the start day. Mentor applications lists the applications in one state, the newest received first and 25 at most (open, the default, which is the queue on the Mentors screen's Waiting for review tab: new, held, asked for more information or waiting for a second opinion; selected, waiting for the course; or lapsed), each by its reference, with the day it was received, its state, the days it has been in that state, the country, the languages, the hours a week and the contribution areas the applicant chose, the teacher answer (yes or no), whether the address is confirmed and the possible duplicate and held marks; with it, how many applications are open, selected and lapsed. The country, the languages and the areas are given only when they are on the application form's own lists: an answer edited by hand to anything else is left out (the country comes back as none), and so are all of them while the site has not synced the list of countries or of contribution teams. One filed as spam, declined or made a mentor is never listed.
  • People come back as record IDs, and never by name - a student is the Students record ID of each track they hold, a mentor is their Mentors record ID, and an applicant is their application's reference, such as MAPP-2026-0007. No answer holds a name, a display name, a login, an email address, a WordPress.org username or profile address, a Slack handle, a tutor's or a mentor's name, a website, or any text a person wrote: not an applicant's free-text answer, not a note, not the accessibility or survey answers, not what the form's checks noticed (but the possible duplicate mark) and not the consent evidence. What you type to find someone, a name or an address, is kept in the log beside the question, cleaned to one line of at most 120 characters, and is never repeated in an answer. Claude cannot say whose a record ID is: an Administrator puts the name to it on the site.
  • Looking a person up - search the ID or the reference where the person is listed. A student's Students record ID goes in Search students on the Student accounts list of the Students screen, which finds the account of every track that holds it, so a student with an account is found there. Any student, with an account or not, is found by the same ID in Search on the roster of the institution that the track names in the answer, on the Institution Dashboard opened through the switcher, in the cohort the track started in: an Administrator's search there reads the Students record ID as well as the name, exactly as the ID is written, and the box's hint lists it. A track that names no institution (its institution comes back null) is on no roster. Its student's account, if there is one, is on the Student accounts list, and the row is listed by its name and status, without its ID, under Rows with no institution on the Sync and storage tab of the Institutions screen. A mentor's Mentors record ID goes in Search mentors on the Mentor accounts list or on the Engagement tab of the Mentors screen; a mentor made by hand, whose account holds no Mentors record ID, comes back with none and is found by username or email address. An application's reference goes in Find by reference, above the views of the Mentors screen's Waiting for review tab: it draws the application whole, with its decisions, whatever its age, except one filed as spam, which it reports as not found. The reference is also printed over the applicant's answers in every view of that tab, but a view draws 50 applications at most: the oldest 50 in Waiting, Asked for more information, Second opinion, Selected (course pending) and Lapsed; in Activated, those still waiting for their Airtable row first, then the most recently made mentors; and, under every view, in Recently decided, the 50 most recently declined or filed as spam, newest first. Find by reference reaches the ones past them, except those filed as spam. A reference is the one the applicant saw on the thank-you page.

The Mail tab

Two sections, headed on the screen Invitations and Recent mail. No settings and no Save: each points to the Emails tool, where the emails are edited and their record is kept.

Invitations waiting to be sent

How many invitations are still waiting to be sent, when any are; they go out a few at a time in the background. What each invitation says, and a test of it sent to your own address, are in WPCredits Program > Tools > Emails, on its Templates tab, which Open the email templates opens. Until 1.122.19 this section had a button for each of the four invitations that emailed you a sample; Send me a test on each template's editor does that now, with the invitation as it is saved.

Recent mail

This section points to WPCredits Program > Tools > Emails, which keeps every email the site sends for 30 days, with Open the email log. When an email failed in the last 30 days, the section says how many and links to them.

The Advanced tab

Eleven settings that change rarely, and whose defaults suit almost every site, in four sections, headed on the screen Pipeline stages, Applications, Agreements and Invitations. Until 1.117.0 they could only be changed in code. Each number field refuses what the save would not keep, so the limits given below are the field's own.

Pipeline stages

  • Institution starting stage - the Current Stage an institution is created at in Airtable when its application is approved, First Contact Made by default, chosen from the Institutions table's Current Stage options. It cannot be left blank: a blank one goes back to its default, and a notice says so.
  • Institution pipeline stages - a checkbox list of the same options, eight of them ticked by default, from First Contact Made to Student. An institution at any of the ticked stages is in the pipeline, and one whose stage leaves the list is treated as having left it, which the Institutions tab's leaving rule decides the rest of. It cannot be left empty, since an empty list would count every institution as having left: an empty one goes back to its default, and a notice says so. When the stages cannot be read, both are typed, the pipeline stages one per line, and a sentence under each says why.

Keeping applications

How long a decided application is kept, institution, sponsor and mentor applications alike, and the one proxy the three application forms believe.

  • Spam kept for (days) - from 1 to 365, 30 by default: an application marked as spam is deleted this many days after it was marked.
  • Rejected kept for (days) - from 30 to 3650, a year by default: a rejected or declined application, or a mentor application that lapsed, is deleted this many days after the decision, and one the checks held, which has no decision, this many days after the last thing that happened to it. Either way the wait is long enough to recognize the same applicant applying again.
  • Approved kept for (days) - from 0 to 3650, 0 by default, which keeps approved applications, and the mentor applications of those who became mentors, forever: they are the record of who was let in. An application made a mentor whose Airtable row is still to be written is kept whatever this says, since Write the Airtable row again needs its answers.
  • Trusted proxy - the one IP address, not a range, of the proxy whose forwarded header the application forms believe for a sender's address, which their limits count by. Its fold: leave it empty unless the site sits behind a proxy, since anybody can send that header; anything but one IP address, a range included, is refused with a notice and the address saved before is kept; clear the box to save it empty.

The daily run that keeps these days for the mentor applications also lapses a selected application whose course has not shown after the days set under Mentor applications on the Students and mentors tab, and what every deleted mentor application counted for the public feed of application figures is kept, so the feed's months do not change as rows go.

Agreement files

  • Largest upload (MB) - from 1 to 50, 10 by default: the largest signed agreement an institution or a sponsor can upload.
  • Uploads per day - from 1 to 50, 5 by default: how many files one institution or one sponsor can upload in a day.
  • Generations per day - from 1 to 100, 10 by default: how many times one institution can generate its agreement from the template in a day.
  • Discarded files kept for (days) - from 7 to 365, 30 by default: a withdrawn or returned file is deleted this many days after it was set aside. An accepted agreement never is.

Lapsed invitations

  • Settled invitations kept for (days) - from 7 to 365, 30 by default: how long an invitation to join an institution's account stays listed once it was accepted, canceled or ran out, so an Administrator can still see who was invited and never came.

Tools you run on their own

Four of the tools keep settings of their own: the Mentor Status Checker, the Student Duplicate Finder, Need help? and Emails. Each shows them in a Settings section at the top of its screen, a form with its own Save settings that saves that tool's settings and nothing else, and the notice after a save, on the same screen, names the tool. The Settings screen's Connection tab names all four, each a link to its section. On the Tools screen, a tool that cannot run says why on its card, in its own words: the Airtable connection for the Mentor Status Checker and the Student Duplicate Finder, and for Need help? its switch or its provider.

Header notices

WPCredits Program > Tools > Header notices. One notice per audience - Students, Mentors, Institutions, Sponsors, Administrators - each in its own editor on one screen, with its own Save this notice button underneath.

  • An empty notice is off. There is no separate switch, because a switch is one more thing to leave in the wrong position.
  • Anyone in two audiences sees both notices. An administrator who also mentors gets the mentor notice and the administrator one, mentor first. Audience membership uses the same tests the dashboards do, so an administrator matched to an Airtable mentor record counts as a mentor even though the sync never gives them the role.
  • A notice appears at the top of the content, which in this program's theme is the top of the dashboard card - not above the site header.
  • A notice may hold anything a WordPress post may hold (links, images, lists, headings); scripts and other markup a post cannot hold are removed on save, so nothing dangerous is stored rather than merely hidden at render time.

Since 1.123.58 each audience's notice has its own Save, so saving one notice never touches another, and a notice changed after you opened the page is not overwritten.

Emails

WPCredits Program > Tools > Emails. The plugin's emails you can edit, by area. One you have not edited is sent as the plugin ships it. Every email the plugin sends ends with the signature and footer. The tool also keeps a record of every email the site sends, for 30 days. Three tabs, Templates, Signature and footer and Log; the tool's own address opens Templates.

Templates

The plugin's emails, grouped by area, each area in a table of its own. There are ten:

  • Invitations: the student's, which since 1.123.61 can carry a line Your first week, step by step: with the address of the Start here page, through the optional placeholder {start_here_link}, left out together with its label while that page is not published (an email already edited keeps its text, and shows as changed in the shipped text until it is reset), the mentor's, which since 1.122.33 carries the welcome a new mentor is sent, and the sponsor's invitation, and the institution's two, one for an institution whose Collaboration Agreement is not on file yet and one for an institution whose agreement is on file.
  • Mentor calls: what the mentor and the students are told about one-to-one calls, group sessions and series of sessions: a booking, a join, a series joined, a session moved, a place left or released, a call or a session canceled, and the reminder a day before. Where the mentor and the student are told different words, each has an email of its own, named for whom it goes to; a group session's cancellation and its reminder say the same words to the mentor and to every student on it, so each is one email. A mentor who has not set a meeting link yet is told so where the others are told where to meet, so the mentor's three confirmations, of a call, of a join and of a series, each have a second email for that case.
  • Institutions: what an institution and the Administrators are told from its application to its last member: the acknowledgement of an application, the notice of it to the Administrators, an Administrator's question and the rejection; a member's invitation to a colleague, and to a colleague as a tutor, who sees the students and changes nothing; the notice to an Administrator that an institution has been assigned to them, unless they made the assignment; the institution's Collaboration Agreement received, uploaded, accepted, put back in force, returned with a note and revoked, the daily list of agreements waiting too long, and the notice that the agreement's template could not be used; the notice that an institution has no members left; and what happens to an institution's details: a correction saved at once, a request to correct a checked detail (its name, website, city, country or contact's email), the request's approval, its decline with the Administrator's note, and its withdrawal. An email that says other words in one case than in another is two: the acknowledgement for a country with a call to book and for one without, the upload with the courtesy scan's notes and without, the revocation with a program contact for the institution's country named and without one, which tells the institution to write to the Administrator who has been in touch, and each invitation with its inviter named and with nobody to name as its sender, the inviter's account gone or holding no name.
  • Semester reports: the notice to the Administrators that the daily job drafted a report, the approval to the institution's accounts, and the question to the students whether the report may mention them.
  • Sponsors: the acknowledgement of a sponsor application (and its twin for an application whose logo files were not kept), the notice of it to the Administrators, an Administrator's question and the rejection; the sponsor's Collaboration Agreement received, accepted, returned with a note, out of force and back in force; what a sponsor says on the Sponsor Dashboard it would like to support, and its request to sponsor a mentor; the warning that an offer's codes are running low and a claimant's report of a code that did not work; a sponsor's post sent back to its author; a sponsor's offer, or a change to a live one, sent back with a note to the member who sent it; and the mail to a sponsor's Administrator thirty days before its term ends, and its twin for a term the daily run finds already over.
  • Sponsor events: what the people on a sponsor's event, or on one of the program's own, the sponsor's accounts and its Administrator are told: a join and a leave, with the calendar file that adds the event or takes it off; a change or a cancel, to the people on it; the reminder the day before, to the people on it and to the sponsor's accounts that are not; an Administrator's approval, return and cancel with a note, to the sponsor's accounts; a change or a cancel of an approved event made on the Sponsor Dashboard, to the sponsor's accounts; and what a sponsor plans, changes or cancels there, to its Administrator. An event of the program's own says "Hosted by the WordPress Credits Program" where a sponsor's names its sponsor, so it has emails of its own, and so has what an Administrator did on a sponsor's behalf through the Sponsor Dashboard's switcher. An event returned with a note to a sponsor whose tier no longer includes events has an email of its own, since the return cancels it.
  • Mentor applications (since 1.122.31): what a person who applied to mentor through the form on the site is told, the acknowledgement with the link that confirms the address, the selection with the mentors' course invitation link, the request for more information and the decline, and the notice of a new application to the Administrators. The four to the applicant ship with the words the program's Airtable automations sent, and carry the program's contact address as their Reply-To when Contact address in emails is set, so an answer reaches the program.
  • Student registrations (since 1.123.54): what a student is told once the registration they sent on the site has an outcome. There are three: the registration was received and written to Airtable, the address already has an account on the site (with the sign-in link and the password reset link), and the address is already registered. Each goes to the address the student gave, once, and carries the program's contact address as its Reply-To when Contact address in emails is set, so an answer reaches the program.
  • Student interests (since 1.123.64): the two emails of the student interest form. The first tells a student that their interest was received, that the program will get in touch with the representative they named and that nothing else is needed from them; it goes to the address the student gave, once, for an interest stored as new or held, and carries the program's contact address as its Reply-To when Contact address in emails is set. The second tells Administrators of a new interest, with the institution's name and country and a link to the Interests tab. No email of this area goes to the representative.
  • Quiet students (since 1.123.60): the three emails of the daily list of quiet students, sent only while the Daily list setting is On. The student gets a friendly note once for each stretch of quiet: how many days since they were last seen, or, for a student not seen since their track started or their account was made, how many days ago that was, each in a sentence of its own with its own placeholder; the mentor's name and the name of the Administrator assigned to their institution, each in a sentence left out for a student who has none; a link to book a call, or, for a student with no mentor and no booking page from that Administrator, who has nothing to book, the address in Contact address in emails; and a link to the Student Report Card, where We've already talked is. The mentor gets one email a day with the students just reminded whose reminder went out, and its subject and first line give their number, so one student reads as right as several. Each Administrator gets one email on Monday with the quiet students of the institutions assigned to them, most quiet first, and a link to the Students gone quiet card. Each list is written in the language of the person it goes to. None says anything about a penalty.

Where an email is two, as the mentor's confirmations with and without a meeting link and the others above are, each of the two is edited on its own: an edit of one leaves the other as shipped. So an Administrator's edit of "Invitation to join an institution" does not carry over to "Invitation to join an institution, with no sender named": that invitation is sent as shipped until it is edited too.

Each row names the email, who receives it and what sends it, its state, and who edited it last and when. The states:

  • Shipped text: the email is sent as the plugin ships it, which is word for word what it said before it could be edited: before 1.122.19 for the Invitations, before 1.122.21 for the Mentor calls and the Semester reports, and before 1.122.22 for the Institutions and the Sponsors, but for what 1.122.23 changed on purpose: the warning that an offer's codes are running low says "1 code left" for one, writes a count past a thousand and the mark beside it alike, and leaves out its Offers card line while the Sponsor Dashboard's page is not published; an institution's Collaboration Agreement sent back or revoked by an Administrator whose account holds no name, or only spaces, says "by an Administrator", and a sponsor's sent back by one says "An Administrator"; the invitation with nobody to name as its sender is an email of its own; an invitation to an institution says that a reply reaches the person who sent it only while it carries their address to reply to; the two emails about what a sponsor would like to support name the site; the notice of an upload the courtesy scan noticed something in says what in words; and every email prints a name as it was typed, its subject included, as below.
  • Edited: it is sent as an Administrator wrote it, to everybody, in that wording.
  • Edited, and the shipped text has changed since: an update changed the shipped text after the edit was saved. The edit is still the one sent, and its editor opens the new shipped text under the buttons, to compare. Saving your edit again clears this state.
  • Edit set aside: the edit uses a placeholder the email no longer has, lacks one it now needs, or has one in its subject that goes in the body, so the shipped text is sent until the edit is saved again; the state says which placeholder.

Edit opens the email's editor: a Subject and a Body, the email's placeholders, each with what it means and an example, and a Preview of the email filled with the examples and ending with the signature and footer. A placeholder, such as {set_password_link}, is a word in braces that is replaced by its value as the email is sent, as a person reads it: a name or a title WordPress stores with an "&" or a "<" written as an entity, an account's name or an application's among them, arrives as it was typed, in the body and in the subject. The subject of every email in this list is plain text since 1.122.23, as an edited one's has been since 1.122.22, so a "<" or an "&" in it is a character, never an entity, and nothing in it that looks like a tag is taken out; a line break in it is one space. A sentence whose placeholders are all empty is left out, and so is a line left with nothing on it, together with the line ending in a colon directly above it when that line holds no placeholder: an invitation with no dashboard page published leaves out the line that would name it, as it always did. A sentence ends at a full stop followed by a space; a question or exclamation mark does not end one. So in "Thanks! Write to {program_contact}." with no contact address set, the whole of it goes, "Thanks!" with it, and in "e.g. " the full stop ends a sentence.

An email about a call shows every time on its recipient's own clock: {when} is the call's start and end as the recipient reads them, and {time_zone} names that clock, so a mentor in Tokyo and a student in Warsaw each read the call at their own hour. A date in an Institutions or a Sponsors email, such as {accepted_on}, is the site's, as it always was. A count arrives in words, such as {session_count}, "3 sessions", or {review_window}, "3 working days", so a template needs no rule for one and several. So does the number of codes left in the warning that an offer's codes are running low, {codes_left}, "3 codes", since 1.122.23, where it arrived as a number: an edit of that email saved before, which says "{codes_left} codes left", reads "3 codes codes left" until it is edited again. Past a thousand, the count and the mark it warns below, {low_mark}, are written alike, "4,999 codes" and "5,000". What the courtesy scan noticed, {scan_flags}, is in words since 1.122.23, each with the PDF's own name for it in brackets, such as "an action that runs when the file is opened (/OpenAction)", in an edit saved before as well; the Institutions screen, the Sponsors screen and the Administrator Dashboard name what the scan noticed in the same words. Both invitations to an institution, the one with its sender named and the one with nobody to name, gain the optional {replies_reach} in 1.122.23, so an edit saved before, which lacks it, is still sent as edited. An invitation to an institution, with its sender named or not, says that a reply reaches the person who sent it, {replies_reach}, only while it carries their address to reply to; empty, its sentence is left out. The two emails about what a sponsor would like to support gain an optional {site_name}, which names the site in their subject, so an edit saved before, which lacks it, is still sent as edited. An edit of an email whose shipped body ends with a line break, as a Semester reports email's does, ends with one too, after its signature and footer.

  • Save stores the subject and the body, and is refused in the cases below.
  • Send me a test, beside Save, sends the email as it is saved, filled with the example values and with "[Test]" before its subject, to your own address and to nobody else. The Log marks it Test. Save what you typed first: pressed with typing not saved yet, it sends nothing, and the editor comes back with your typing and says so. A test carries the subject and the body alone: the calendar file a Mentor calls email carries, and the reply address that several emails go out with (a Mentor calls email, an Administrator's question to an applicant, an agreement sent back with a note, a sponsor's agreement taken out of force, a colleague's invitation, a code that did not work), are added when it is really sent, so a test of one arrives without them.
  • Restore the original is there once the email is edited. It asks first, then drops the edit, and the shipped text is sent from then on.

Save is refused, nothing is stored, and the editor comes back with what you typed, when:

  • a box is empty;
  • a required placeholder is missing. Each email's required placeholders are marked Required in its editor's placeholder table; the ones below are the common ones, not the full list. Every invitation needs {set_password_link}, the link that sets the password, and so does every other link that carries a secret: an institution application's confirmation link, {verify_link}, and a colleague's invitation to an institution, {accept_link}. Every email about a call needs {when}, its time (a series, {session_dates}), and a semester report {semester}. What an Administrator or a sponsor wrote, where it is the email's point, is needed too: a question to an applicant, {question}; a note on a returned or revoked agreement or a returned post, {note}; and what a sponsor said, {interest}. A returned post needs its title and its author's name, {post_title} and {author_name}, either of which can be empty. And an email sent only with a value its other words lack needs it: the mentor's confirmation sent with a meeting link, {meeting_place}; the acknowledgement with a call to book, {booking_link}; the upload with the scan's notes, {scan_flags}; the revocation with a country contact, {country_contact};
  • a link or a typed text that goes in the body is in the subject: a link that carries a secret, a mentor's meeting link, {meeting_place}, which can carry the meeting's passcode, a code's last characters, {code_ending}, what a person typed, such as {topic}, {question} or {note}, or an applicant's own answers (an address, a website, a contact, a city). A subject is not a link anybody can follow, and the Log keeps it;
  • a placeholder is not one of the email's (a misspelled one is named as one the email does not have; a misspelled required one is reported as missing instead);
  • WordPress would remove part of the text; or
  • the subject is longer than 200 characters or the body longer than 10,000.

A save of the shipped text as it stands stores nothing, so the email stays shipped text. A subject made of placeholders alone, such as {mentor_name}, is saved; if they all come out empty, the email goes out with its shipped subject rather than with none, since an email with no subject is not sent.

Since 1.123.58 an email somebody changed after you opened it is not overwritten: the editor says who changed it and when, and keeps your wording in the boxes. An email restored to the shipped text after you opened the page is refused the same way.

Signature and footer

The one block every email the plugin sends ends with, after a blank line and a line holding -- . It is not added to the emails WordPress and the Two Factor plugin send themselves. Its placeholders are {site_name}; {site_link}, the site's public address, its home page, the same for everyone (since 1.122.37), which is left out of an email that names the home page already; {dashboard_link}, the recipient's dashboard, which is empty for somebody with no account, such as an applicant, and for an email that names the dashboard already, as every invitation does, so its line is left out and no email names the address twice; and {program_contact}, the address in Contact address in emails, which is empty until it is set, so its sentence is left out. A line left with nothing is left out whole, so no email has an empty line in its footer. It ships as four lines (the site's address since 1.123.24):

  • WordPress Credits, WordPress Education
  • {site_link}
  • {dashboard_link}
  • This email comes from the WordPress Credits program. Questions? Write to {program_contact}.

{dashboard_link} is each person's own page: a student's Student Report Card, a mentor's Mentor Report Card, an institution member's Institution Dashboard, a sponsor member's Sponsor Dashboard and an Administrator's Administrator Dashboard. A page that is not published gives no link. The tab's preview and Send me a test show the footer as an Administrator gets it, since the test goes to you, so both show the Administrator Dashboard; a note under the preview, and the test itself, list what everybody else gets. The site's address, on the line above, is the same in every email, and everybody can open it, an applicant with no account among them. A site whose front page is one of the dashboards prints that address once, on the site's line.

The tab edits it with the editor every template has, without a subject, with Save and Send me a test (a short email that ends with the block); once the block has been edited, Restore the original appears too. An empty block is not saved, since every email ends with it.

Settings

At the top of the Signature and footer tab, the tool's one setting, Contact address in emails: a mailbox the Administrators read, which the footer names for questions. Left empty, the footer leaves that sentence out. An address that is not one is not saved, and the tab says so.

Log

A record of every email the site sends, kept for 30 days: the plugin's own, WordPress's (a password reset, for example) and the Two Factor plugin's sign-in codes. Use it to answer "did they get the email?".

Each row is one recipient of one email: when it was sent, in the site's time zone; the address as plain text, and under it the person's name when the address belonged to an account at the time. The name links, for as long as the account exists, to the person's row on the Accounts tab of the screen for the role the account holds now (Students, Mentors, Institutions, Sponsors or Administrators), where the person's actions are (Send invite and Resend invite on every screen but Administrators, whose accounts are never invited), found by the account's email address as it is now; an account with no program role links to its user editor, and a row with no account is plain text. Then the recipient type (Student, Mentor, Institution member, Sponsor member, Administrator, Applicant (no account) or Other); the area that sent it (Invitations, Mentor calls, Institutions, Semester reports, Sponsors, Sponsor events, Mentor applications, Student registrations, Student interests, Quiet students, WordPress, Two Factor or Other); which email it was; its subject; and its status. The status is one of three:

  • Handed to the mail server: the site passed the email on. This does not prove it reached the inbox: a full mailbox or a spam filter can still stop it after it leaves the site.
  • Failed: WordPress could not hand it over; the reason it gave is shown under the status.
  • Not confirmed: another plugin took the email over before WordPress could say what happened, or the request ended, with a fatal error for example, before it did.

A Test mark beside the status shows a test you sent yourself with Send me a test (or, before 1.122.19, a sample from Settings > Mail). It is not a fourth status: the test has one of the three as well, and the Status filter has a Test choice that lists the tests.

To find an email, type part of an address, a name or a subject into the search box, or narrow the list by Area, Recipient type, Status, Email or When (today, the last 7 days, the last 30 days, or from and to dates), and press Filter. The Email filter is one field: type a few letters of the email's name and pick it from the list. Fifty rows show a page, newest first, with the count above them. Until 1.122.21 the Mentor calls emails were named by five names that each covered the mentor's copy and the students' alike, such as Call booked and Call reminder; the rows sent before keep those names, which now end "(until 1.122.21)", for the 30 days the log keeps them. Until 1.122.22 a Collaboration Agreement put back in force was logged as an acceptance and a sponsor's request to sponsor a mentor as Sponsor interest; each has a name of its own since. The institution's agreement emails, the rows sent before included, are named for the Collaboration Agreement in full, such as Collaboration Agreement accepted, to the institution, and the sponsor's five agreement emails say who receives them, such as Collaboration Agreement accepted, to the sponsor.

The log never keeps the text of an email, its attachments, or anything secret such as a sign-in code or a password link. Entries older than 30 days are deleted every day. WordPress's Export Personal Data and Erase Personal Data tools include a person's entries, found by their address. Erasing a person's entries is followed by WordPress's own confirmation email to that address, and the log records that email too, so a fresh row for the address after an erasure is expected. The emails the plugin had recorded before 1.122.18 (Settings > Mail showed the last 25 of up to a hundred) move into the log, with their addresses masked as they were kept, no subject and no recipient type; those older than 30 days are deleted with the rest.

Mentor Status Checker

WPCredits Program > Tools > Mentor Status Checker. Reads the WordPress.org profile of each mentor who has still to be made one, matches the Credits Mentor's Course completion. Run check (report only) shows what it would change without changing anything; Run check and promote to Active changes mentors as it goes, after one confirmation. It has two sources. First the applications selected on this site, the newest selection first: where the course shows on an applicant's profile, they are made a mentor on this site, once Make mentors from applications is on (see Applications to mentor in the part on the plugin in wp-admin). Then, until Stop checking mentors in Airtable is ticked, the mentors whose Airtable status is the one set under Check mentors with status, Vetted - positive by default: where the course shows on one of those profiles, they are promoted to Active in Airtable, as they were before 1.122.33.

It needs the Airtable connection only for Airtable's mentors. The applications selected on this site are checked without it; while Airtable is not connected, the tool's status line and its screen say that Airtable's mentors are not checked, and that a mentor made from an application gets no Airtable row until it is. A run in which Airtable cannot be read still checks the site's applications, and says above its results that Airtable's mentors were left out of it; with no application selected, the error is the answer, as it was when Airtable was the only source.

An application's row in the results reads Made a mentor once it is, with what was held or not written on the way (an invitation held, an Airtable row refused), and the tally counts made a mentor beside promoted. A run that only reports, and any run while Make mentors from applications is off, makes nobody a mentor: an application whose course shows reads Awaiting promotion, "Ready to be made a mentor", or, while the switch is off, Waiting, with "it waits until Make mentors from applications is switched on". A report keeps on each application the day of its last check, which the Selected view shows. Run check and promote to Active (the last word is the status set under Promote them to) and Promote all eligible promote and make mentors from both sources, and Promote on one row re-checks that mentor or application first, never from the cache, and refuses an application that has left Selected (course pending). A row that reads Waiting offers no Promote, since it says it waits; the summary above the results counts those rows as waiting for Make mentors from applications, apart from those awaiting promotion, as the tool's status line does, and Promote all eligible leaves them out. Once the switch is on, the same rows await promotion again. One that Promote all eligible finds has left Selected (course pending) since the run comes back as failed under the applicant's name, with the reason.

Since 1.123.58 Promote keeps the keyboard's place on the promoted row and says who was promoted; a run's progress is said at each quarter and at the end. A row that was not promoted has its reason said, and Promote all says how many were promoted and moves the keyboard's place to the first of them.

Settings

At the top of the checker's screen, above the buttons that start a run, a form with its own Save settings:

The Slack message after a promotion

With a webhook saved, every action that promotes or makes a mentor sends one message once it has finished: a run, whether the daily one, Run check and promote to Active or wp wpcredits check_mentors --promote; Promote all eligible; Promote on one row; or, since 1.122.33, The course is completed on an application, which sends its message at once. It calls the channel (@channel), says how many mentors were moved to the status they were promoted to and which channel to add them to, and lists each one with a link to their WordPress.org profile and, where the profile shows one, their Slack name, which is the name to type when adding them, shown as code so that an address typed there is not a link. The line of a mentor made from an application ends from an application on the site, and the count and the status in the first line cover them as they cover a promotion. The last line says who promoted: the daily check, WP-CLI or the administrator who pressed the button. Only mentors whose status was actually written, and applicants actually made mentors, are named: an applicant is named as soon as the account is made, so one whose Airtable row was refused is named all the same, and one filed as already a mentor is not. An action that moved nobody sends nothing, and a long list goes in messages of 25. The message is in the site's language, whoever pressed the button.

A message Slack refuses, or that cannot reach Slack, is not lost. Its mentors are kept and sent with the next message, and every run sends what is kept even when it promotes nobody, so with the daily check on a mentor waits a day at most. A mentor promoted while another message was being sent goes in a message of its own about a minute later. A promotion never waits on Slack: Airtable is written first. The line under the buttons says when the last message went and how many it named, or why it failed, and how many still wait. Promotions made while no webhook is saved are not announced later.

Student Duplicate Finder

WPCredits Program > Tools > Student Duplicate Finder. Lists every student who has more than one row in Students, Students Reports or Feedback in Airtable, proposes which rows to delete, and deletes the ones you tick and confirm.

A second row usually comes from the Airtable automation that creates a student's Students Reports and Feedback rows. It runs whenever a Students row starts matching its conditions and it never checks the address, so it runs again for an address that already has rows: a student who did not move forward applies again, or somebody sets a status back and the automation fires a second time. Duplicated addresses are what break the update automations, which is the error you see in Airtable.

The finder clears duplicates up; it does not stop them being made. Stopping them at source is a change to that Airtable automation, written up step by step in Stopping duplicate students at the source.

Delete duplicates here, not by hand in Airtable

This is the part worth reading twice. The site stores Airtable record IDs, and deleting the row one of them names is not something Airtable can warn you about:

  • a student's account holds the record ID of their Students Reports row, which is how their Student Report Card finds their program, and of their Feedback row, which is how their surveys are found;
  • a mentor's call note and a booked call hold the record ID of the student they are about;
  • audit log entries hold the record IDs of what they describe.

Delete such a row in Airtable and the site is left pointing at nothing. For the student, that means their Student Report Card stops showing their program, and there is no message anywhere saying why, on either side.

The finder knows every one of those references. It reads them before it proposes anything, it refuses to delete a row that anything on the site points at, and it checks again in the second before it deletes. That is the whole reason to use it rather than the Airtable interface. If you have already deleted rows by hand and a student now sees nothing, say so: the site can be pointed at the surviving row again, but only by someone who knows which row that was.

What a scan does

A scan reads the three tables and writes nothing to Airtable, so running one is always safe.

  • It runs by itself every three hours, at a different minute from the students, mentors and institutions syncs, so no two of them run in the same request.
  • Scan now runs one while you watch, with a progress bar. Press it if you have just changed something in Airtable and want the list to catch up.
  • A scan that fails changes nothing, whether Airtable did not answer or the site could not read which of its own records point at the rows. Its error appears above the list, and the last good list stays on screen, so a bad night never leaves you with an empty screen.
  • An address is the same student however it is typed. Capitals and spaces before or after it make no difference, so a row whose address was typed with a space around it is listed, and can be deleted, like any other. When a student's rows spell the address differently, their card says so.
  • While a scan is running, Scan now is replaced by the progress bar and Cancel scan; a Scan now pressed from a page opened earlier does nothing except say a scan is already running. Review selection is disabled while a scan is running, because the rows underneath the list are about to change.

Working through the list

  1. Open the finder and read the tiles: how many students are duplicated, how many are Ready, how many need a decision, and, for each table, how many rows are proposed for deletion and how many are held.
  2. Start with Ready. Press Select all ready, or tick students one at a time.
  3. Move on to needs a decision. Each row that may go has its own checkbox and, beside it, the sentence saying why it was held back. Read the sentence and decide. Nothing is ever ticked for you here.
  4. Press Review selection. Nothing has been deleted yet.
  5. The confirmation lists exactly what will go, table by table, and lists anything it left out with the reason. Rows that would leave a student with no row in a table are left out here already, not only after you press Delete. Read it. This is the page to turn back from.
  6. Press Delete 3 rows from Airtable, where the number is the count of rows the confirmation lists. Only this button deletes anything.

Take it in small batches the first few times. One confirmation deletes at most 100 rows, and there is no prize for clearing the list in one afternoon.

Why a row is held back

The finder keeps the newest row in each table and proposes the older ones, but only when the older row has nothing worth keeping on it. When it does, you get the sentence instead of a proposal:

A student is Ready only when every table's older rows are clean deletes. One held row anywhere moves the whole student to needs a decision, which is why that group is the larger one.

What happens when you press Delete

  • Every row is read from Airtable again and every question is asked again. A row that changed since the scan, that the site has started pointing at, or that is already gone is left out and named on the notice. A row has changed when it carries more work, answers or hours than the list showed, when a value that held it back was replaced (a grade, a note, a screenshot), or when it gained a reason to be kept that it did not have.
  • One delete runs at a time. A Delete pressed while another is running deletes nothing and says so; review the selection again once the first has finished. After a delete that was cut off part of the way, by a timeout for instance, the same notice can show for up to five minutes from when that delete began.
  • If the site cannot read what on it points at the rows, nothing is deleted, and the notice says so.
  • The last row an address has in a table is never deleted. Whatever else happens, a student cannot be erased from a table entirely.
  • Rows go in order: Feedback, then Students Reports, then Students, so a child row never outlives its parent.
  • A sealed copy of every row is written to the site first. If any copy cannot be written, or the site cannot encrypt, nothing in the selection is deleted.
  • If Airtable stops a delete part of the way, the notice says what was deleted before it stopped, with Airtable's own message. The rows it did not confirm stay in the list and can be selected and deleted again; each still ends with one copy and one log entry.

Deleted rows, and the 30-day copy

The Deleted rows list under the students records who deleted which row, from which table, and when. View copy shows that row's cells exactly as they were, so you can type them back into Airtable by hand.

There is no automatic restore. Bringing a row back is a manual job, and a restored row gets a new record ID, so anything that pointed at the old one still needs fixing. After 30 days the cells are erased and the entry stays without a name or an address, as a permanent record that something was deleted.

An entry whose delete Airtable did not confirm says so, and the daily run checks it again: a row still in Airtable leaves the list, copy and all, since nothing was deleted, and a row that is gone becomes an ordinary entry. A copy whose delete Airtable never confirmed is erased at 30 days too, and its entry says the row may still be in Airtable. Look its record ID up there: if the row is still there, the next scan lists it again.

Settings

Deleting ships switched off. Its one setting, Deleting duplicates, with its box Let administrators delete the duplicated rows they select and confirm, is in the Settings section at the top of the finder's screen, above the list, with a Save of its own. Until an Administrator turns it on there, the whole list is read-only: no checkbox can be ticked, Review selection is grayed out, and the list says where deleting is turned on. Scanning and reading work either way, so the list is worth looking at long before anyone decides to delete from it. The row's fold says what a delete does: it removes rows from Students, Students Reports and Feedback in the shared base, and the finder keeps a sealed copy of each row for 30 days.

Leaving it off between clean-ups is a reasonable habit, not a sign that something is wrong.

On the Administrator Dashboard

The Duplicated students tile counts the students the last scan listed, and its card links here. With none listed there is no tile; the card says whether the last scan found nothing or no scan has run yet.

Track Builder

WPCredits Program > Tools > Track Builder. A program track is one Airtable status, one form on the Student Report Card, a key chip in one color and, when the track follows one, a Learn course and an hours target. Before the Track Builder, a new track was a plugin release. Now it is a draft you write here, preview, publish to Airtable and switch on, with no developer in the loop.
